Mr. Charles J. Onlebeke
prototype total energy fuel cell installation was made in a single family dwelling in Farmington, Connecticut, as part of a nine-year research and development program conducted under the auspices of the Team to Advance Research for Gas Energy Transformation. Present plans are that this installation is to be followed by 31 other installations in various parts of the country and in different applications. Upon the conclusion of this program operating experience should be available to provide a basis of judging the practical and economic feasibility of generating electricity in relatively small fuel cells using natural gas and other suitable substances to provide the input energy.
While it is often unwise to anticipate result of research and development, it is difficult to overlook contagious optimism of fuelcell sponsors or to underestimate the profound changes that could result from successful fuel cell applications or the wide range of benefits which can result from reduction in the number of conventional fossil fuel combustion operations for space heating and electricity generation. A successful fuel-cell module of 10 to 15 kilowatts, envisioned for single family residences, could be coupled in banks to serve larger users. Looking to the larger applications, the fuel cell because of its modular capability and the possibility of tailoring power output to a specific customer's needs, could find broad application in all sizes of commercial and apartment complexes. Since the fuel cell would not be dependent on electric transmission and distribution networks, successful conclusion of the current experiments would permit significant future environmental advantages. Furthermore, fuel cell installations in the future which eliminate the need for a multiplicity of small conventional fuel combustion operations augur well for a general benefaction of air quality in urban centers which are currently faced with difficult air pollution problems.
We have tried to indicate that total energy systems are not new; that considerable experience has been accumulated in the operation of these systems; and that total energy systems are not necessarily more efficient on an annual basis than other electrical systems. We have also noted promising advances which are currently being made in fuel cell technology in application to residential and possibly larger commercial loads.
Sincerely,
John N. Nassikas
floor better
Chairman
